Question: The equation \(\sqrt{x+4}-\sqrt{x-3}+1=0\) has:

Choices.C: one real root and one imaginary root

Solution:
For real \(x\), both square roots are defined exactly when \(x\ge3\). Throughout this domain, \(x+4>x-3\ge0\). A larger nonnegative number has a larger principal square root, so
\[
\sqrt{x+4}-\sqrt{x-3}+1>1.
\]
Thus there are no real roots, including at the endpoint \(x=3\).

Because the choices also mention imaginary roots, we should rule out nonreal solutions. Any solution would satisfy
\[
\sqrt{x+4}=\sqrt{x-3}-1.
\]
Squaring makes the \(x\)-terms cancel:
\[
x+4=x-3-2\sqrt{x-3}+1,
\]
which gives \(\sqrt{x-3}=-3\). Squaring again forces \(x-3=9\), so every possible solution must be \(x=12\). In particular, no nonreal value can be a solution.

Squaring can introduce false candidates, so we must check \(12\) in the original equation. With the usual principal square roots, its left side is
\[
\sqrt{16}-\sqrt9+1=4-3+1=2\ne0.
\]
The only candidate fails. Therefore the equation has no root, choice \(\boxed{\text{A}}\).
